claims.text: Adding approximately 20 vol% SiC to ZrB2 and consolidating it by spark plasma sintering below 1700 °C will produce a dense composite.
The ZrB2–SiC composite will have greater oxidation resistance than single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature monolithic specimens.
The ZrB2–SiC composite will have greater liquid-metal corrosion resistance than single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature monolithic specimens.
The enhanced oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion resistance arises from a protective silica-rich scale.
The starting monolithic ZrB2 powder has minimal oxide contamination and a typical sub-micron particle size.
Moderate uniaxial pressure during SPS at 1600–1700 °C is sufficient for full densification.
The added SiC remains as a secondary phase in the consolidated body.
The secondary SiC phase forms a protective silica scale in oxidizing environments.
The SiC-derived scale restricts molten-metal penetration in plating environments.
Silicon from SiC preferentially oxidizes during high-temperature exposure.
Preferential silicon oxidation creates a dense silica layer that inhibits oxygen diffusion.
The dense silica layer inhibits liquid-metal infiltration.
SiC particles facilitate lower-temperature densification by enhancing diffusion and eliminating residual porosity.
Adding SiC will lower the ZrB2 densification temperature by approximately 600–700 °C.
The composite will retain higher strength and undergo less mass change during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Single-phase ZrB2 requires at least 2300 °C for full densification.
Single-phase ZrB2 oxidizes and corrodes faster than the proposed composite under the same service conditions.
Previous methods using sintering temperatures near 1700 °C produced bodies with reduced structural integrity or oxidation/corrosion durability.
The proposed composite is applicable in oxidizing service environments up to approximately 1500–1600 °C.
The proposed composite is applicable to prolonged service in hazardous liquid-metal plating baths.

contradictions.description: The core hypothesis requires sintering below 1700 °C and the falsification rule requires T < 1700 °C, but the stated processing range includes 1700 °C and the experimental composite is specified as being sintered at approximately 1700 °C.
